# Education in New Zealand
Education in New Zealand is characterized by a structured, inclusive, and government-funded system covering early childhood, primary, secondary, and tertiary levels. Early childhood education includes both teacher-led and parent-led options, with services required to follow the Te Whāriki curriculum framework and be licensed by the Ministry of Education. Primary and secondary education are free for New Zealand citizens and residents, and compulsory from ages 6 to 16, though most students start at age 5 and stay until at least age 17. There are 13 year levels, with the school year running from late January to mid-December and divided into four terms.
School types include state schools (government-owned and free, though donations are solicited), state-integrated schools (retaining a special character and charging compulsory attendance dues), and private schools (fee-based with limited government funding). School governance relies on elected Boards of Trustees. The curriculum is standardized nationally, with NCEA as the main qualification, and alternative frameworks (IB, CIE) also offered. Māori language education has seen revitalization and increased availability through immersion schools, contributing to improved outcomes for Māori students. Specialist schools exist for disabled and special needs students.
Tertiary education is regulated by the New Zealand Qualifications Framework, with funding from government grants and student fees. Students can access loans and allowances for living and tuition costs. Tertiary pathways include universities and vocational institutions. Educational standards have faced criticism, particularly in mathematics, and disparities persist for Māori and Pacific Island students. Bullying in schools remains a challenge despite government intervention. School enrolment zoning aims to manage access fairly, but property values and parental actions influence school choice. Overall, the system emphasizes accessibility, government funding, a standardized curriculum, and attention to linguistic and cultural diversity, especially for Māori learners.
